# Overview

<cite id="a6534cb5-0">Skin integrates passive protection with active immune surveillance: when intact, it blocks pathogen entry while housing resident immune cells that detect threats and mount responses in both epidermis and dermis</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-2">The epidermis forms the foremost physical barrier (notably the stratum corneum) while underlying immune cells—including Langerhans cells and diverse dermal dendritic cells and lymphocytes—create an active immunological microenvironment</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-1">Keratinocytes act as immune sentinels by sensing danger via pattern-recognition receptors and cooperating with antigen-presenting cells to initiate antigen-specific adaptive immunity</cite>.

# Physical barrier: structure, junctions, and barrier lipids

<cite id="dbe39e72-1">The stratum corneum adopts a “brick-and-mortar” architecture: flattened, terminally differentiated corneocytes (rich in filaggrin and keratin macrofibrils) are embedded in an intercellular lamellar lipid matrix of cholesterol, ceramides, free fatty acids, and wax esters</cite>. <cite id="dbe39e72-1">Corneocytes are encased in a cornified cell envelope (a dense keratin layer) and interconnected by corneodesmosomes, while intracellular natural moisturizing factors contribute to hydration and desquamation</cite>. <cite id="dbe39e72-1">Below, tight junctions in stratum granulosum keratinocytes add a secondary paracellular barrier that complements the corneum, and alterations in chemical or microbial conditions can perturb both junctions and the corneum barrier</cite>.

<cite id="dbe39e72-0">The stratum corneum surface is coated by an acidic “acid mantle” (low pH) that is essential for barrier formation, anti-microbial defense, and barrier repair, with barrier regeneration proceeding rapidly at acidic pH and slowing markedly at neutral pH due to reduced glycosidase activity and lamellar lipid secretion</cite>. <cite id="d472a63-2">Barrier lipids are synthesized and secreted via lamellar bodies from basal keratinocytes into the suprabasal layers; perturbing these lipids or their lamellar organization severely impairs barrier function</cite>. <cite id="d472a63-2">Cholesterol and its sulfate ester, together with long-chain ceramides and fatty acids, pack tightly to stabilize the lipid bilayers and maintain skin cohesion; cholesterol sulfate can stabilize corneodesmosomes and support lamellar assembly</cite>.

# Chemical defenses: innate molecules and sweat

<cite id="3cc12346-2">Skin deploys antimicrobial peptides and proteins—especially cathelicidins and β/γ-defensins—as a central antimicrobial barrier; these small cationic polypeptides directly kill microbes and also bridge innate and adaptive immunity by activating immune cells, influencing cytokines/chemokines, chemotaxis, epithelial proliferation, and wound healing</cite>. <cite id="3cc12346-2">Dermcidin is constitutively produced by eccrine sweat glands and present at 1–10 µg/ml on the skin surface, with further post-secretory processing in sweat to active forms</cite>. <cite id="3cc12346-1">LL-37 (processed from hCAP-18) and β-defensins 1–2 increase during inflammation (e.g., psoriasis) and are detectable in sweat, where LL-37 undergoes additional proteolytic processing that enhances its activity</cite>.

<cite id="3cc12346-2">Lipid mediators also contribute: free fatty acids (e.g., lauric, palmitic, oleic), sphingosine, glucosylceramides, and hydrolytic ceramide fragments possess intrinsic antimicrobial activity and serve as danger signals that amplify defenses by inducing antimicrobial peptide expression in sebocytes and other epithelial cells</cite>. <cite id="3cc12346-0">Free fatty acids from skin lipids upregulate human β-defensin expression in sebocytes and synergize with cathelicidin and LL-37 against Gram-positive, Gram-negative bacteria, and yeast, illustrating cooperative interactions between antimicrobial lipids and proteins</cite>. <cite id="3cc12346-2">These chemical barriers are localized and delivered to the stratum corneum: AMPs are synthesized in suprabasal layers and stored in lamellar bodies for delivery to the corneum, aligning barrier formation with antimicrobial action</cite>.

# Immune cells and systems: who does what, where

<cite id="a6534cb5-0">Innate and adaptive components reside in epidermis and dermis: Langerhans cells and keratinocytes initiate immune recognition in the epidermis, while the dermis houses mast cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells within organized micro-anatomical niches</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-1">Keratinocytes express toll-like receptors and other PAMP-sensing receptors, enabling them to detect microbial products, sense injury, and switch to an “activation” state that coordinates epithelial and immune responses</cite>.

<cite id="a6534cb5-2">Langerhans cells are epidermal-resident sentinel antigen-presenting cells that sample environmental insults, capture antigens by extending dendrites through tight junctions, emigrate to lymph nodes, and initiate adaptive immunity by triggering antigen-specific T-cell proliferation</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-1">Dermal antigen-presenting cells include conventional dendritic cells (cDC1 and cDC2) that bridge innate sensing to adaptive responses; the dermis also contains γδ T cells, innate lymphoid cells, CD4+ T cells, neutrophils, macrophages, and mast cells, collectively forming a dynamic immune network for rapid response</cite>.

<cite id="a6534cb5-0">Resident memory T cells and dendritic epidermal immune cells (including IDEC subsets) localize in the epidermis and dermal-epidermal junction, coordinating early detection and response to recurrent threats at portals of entry</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-0">Non-hematopoietic sentinels such as keratinocytes and fibroblasts also trigger and shape immunity: keratinocyte danger sensing and cytokine/chemokine production recruit immune cells, while fibroblasts in the dermis secrete mediators that guide leukocyte function and tissue repair</cite>.

<cite id="a6534cb5-0">Immune cells cooperate closely: skin mast cells and dendritic cells collaborate with T cells and keratinocytes to prime and drive responses, and during wound healing, coordinated immune and non-immune cell activity clears pathogens, debrides necrotic tissue, and programs tissue regeneration</cite>.

# Integration across layers: sensing, signaling, and crosstalk

<cite id="a6534cb5-1">Keratinocyte PRRs (e.g., TLRs) and alarmins link microbial sensing to cytokine and chemokine production that recruit and activate dendritic cells and leukocytes, while epidermal injury signals induce keratinocyte gene programs that reinforce barrier sealing and immune alerting</cite>. <cite id="3cc12346-2">Antimicrobial peptides are immunomodulators: they activate epithelial and immune cells, promote cytokine/chemokine production and neutrophil chemotaxis, and coordinate epithelial proliferation and wound repair alongside innate killing</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-2">Langerhans cells bridge the epidermis and adaptive immunity by migrating to lymph nodes to present captured antigens, while tissue-resident memory T cells stationed in the epidermis provide rapid recall responses at likely sites of invasion</cite>.

<cite id="a6534cb5-2">The dermis integrates diverse immune cells—macrophages, dendritic subsets, ILCs, mast cells, T cells—arranged around vessels and extracellular matrix to rapidly initiate inflammation and tissue defense</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-0">During insults or healing, mast cells, dendritic cells, T cells, and keratinocytes jointly orchestrate pathogen clearance, inflammation resolution, and tissue restoration, with fibroblasts and cytokines shaping the reparative milieu</cite>.

# Barrier disruption, disease, and immune dysregulation

<cite id="3cc12346-2">Disrupted barrier function in diseases such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis is accompanied by altered antimicrobial peptide expression: LL-37, hBD-2, and hBD-3 are upregulated in psoriatic lesions, reflecting heightened innate antimicrobial activity</cite>. <cite id="dbe39e72-1">Because tight junction integrity and the cornified envelope are essential for barrier sealing, perturbations in junction proteins, desmosomes, or lamellar lipid organization impair cohesion, hydration, and paracellular barrier control</cite>.

<cite id="a6534cb5-0">When the physical barrier is compromised (e.g., by injury or disease), the immune network in epidermis and dermis is activated: resident dendritic cells and keratinocyte danger signals promote adaptive responses, but dysregulated inflammation can perpetuate tissue damage</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-2">Tissue-resident memory T cells in the epidermis provide durable local protection, but their persistence in inflamed states can also sustain immune reactivity</cite>.

# Practical implications and summary

- Physical: <cite id="dbe39e72-1">The brick-and-mortar stratum corneum (filaggrin-rich corneocytes in lamellar lipid “mortar”) plus tight junctions in granular layer forms a multilayered barrier that prevents entry and transepidermal water loss</cite>. <cite id="dbe39e72-0">Acidic pH and lamellar lipid assembly are indispensable for barrier regeneration and antimicrobial efficacy</cite>.

- Chemical: <cite id="3cc12346-2">Antimicrobial peptides (cathelicidins/defensins), sweat-borne dermcidin/LL-37, and lipid mediators (free fatty acids, sphingolipids) provide direct microbial killing, chemotaxis, and induction of epithelial and immune responses</cite>. <cite id="3cc12346-2">AMPs are epidermally synthesized and delivered to the corneum via lamellar bodies, coupling barrier and antimicrobial functions</cite>.

- Immune cells/systems: <cite id="a6534cb5-0">Keratinocytes and Langerhans cells initiate detection and antigen handling in the epidermis</cite>; <cite id="a6534cb5-1">dermal dendritic cells, macrophages, γδ T cells, ILCs, and T cells form a rapid-response network that integrates danger signals with adaptive immunity</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-2">Langerhans cells migrate to lymph nodes to prime antigen-specific T cells, and epidermal tissue-resident memory T cells provide immediate recall protection</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-0">During healing, coordinated immune–non-immune cell activity clears infection and guides repair</cite>.

Taken together, <cite id="a6534cb5-0">the skin’s immune system is a layered, integrated defense: physical and chemical barriers limit exposure and kill invaders at the surface</cite>, while <cite id="a6534cb5-2">resident sentinels and organized dermal immune networks detect danger, mount adaptive responses, and restore homeostasis</cite>, with <cite id="3cc12346-2">antimicrobial peptides and lipid-mediated signals linking barrier integrity, microbial control, and immune education</cite>.

In this barrier layer, the "bricks" are terminally differentiated keratinocytes (corneocytes) composed mostly offilaggrin and a dense network of keratin macrofibrils, which is a protein that helps to keep the skin hydrated by preventing water evaporation and absorbing water. The corneocytes are surrounded by an insoluble cornified cell envelope which results in keratinization and is composed of a monolayer of ceramides. These cells are held together in the lipid matrix by corneodesmosomes, modified desmosomes from the uppermost nucleated epidermal layers. Also, intracellular humectants (natural moisturizing factors) that are essential for stratum corneum hydration, barrier homeostasis and desquamation localize in the corneocytes [8,9]. 

The "mortar" includes intercellular lipids arranged into lamellar layers consisting of cholesterol, free fatty acids, approximately ceramides (CERs) and sterol/wax esters. The intercellular lipid lamellar matrix of stratum corneum is essential for maintaining skin barrier function and preventing transepidermal water loss (TEWL) [1,10]. 

Besides the structures of the stratum corneum, the tight junctions attached to lateral walls of keratinocytes in the stratum granulosum have presented a secondary functional barrier in the skin. # Physical barrier: structure, junctions, and barrier lipids

<cite id="dbe39e72-1">The stratum corneum adopts a “brick-and-mortar” architecture: flattened, terminally differentiated corneocytes (rich in filaggrin and keratin macrofibrils) are embedded in an intercellular lamellar lipid matrix of cholesterol, ceramides, free fatty acids, and wax esters</cite>. <cite id="dbe39e72-1">Corneocytes are encased in a cornified cell envelope (a dense keratin layer) and interconnected by corneodesmosomes, while intracellular natural moisturizing factors contribute to hydration and desquamation</cite>. <cite id="dbe39e72-1">Below, tight junctions in stratum granulosum keratinocytes add a secondary paracellular barrier that complements the corneum, and alterations in chemical or microbial conditions can perturb both junctions and the corneum barrier</cite>.

<cite id="a6534cb5-1">Keratinocyte PRRs (e.g., TLRs) and alarmins link microbial sensing to cytokine and chemokine production that recruit and activate dendritic cells and leukocytes, while epidermal injury signals induce keratinocyte gene programs that reinforce barrier sealing and immune alerting</cite>. <cite id="3cc12346-2">Antimicrobial peptides are immunomodulators: they activate epithelial and immune cells, promote cytokine/chemokine production and neutrophil chemotaxis, and coordinate epithelial proliferation and wound repair alongside innate killing</cite>. <cite id="a6534cb5-2">Langerhans cells bridge the epidermis and adaptive immunity by migrating to lymph nodes to present captured antigens, while tissue-resident memory T cells stationed in the epidermis provide rapid recall responses at likely sites of invasion</cite>.

- Physical: <cite id="dbe39e72-1">The brick-and-mortar stratum corneum (filaggrin-rich corneocytes in lamellar lipid “mortar”) plus tight junctions in granular layer forms a multilayered barrier that prevents entry and transepidermal water loss</cite>. <cite id="dbe39e72-0">Acidic pH and lamellar lipid assembly are indispensable for barrier regeneration and antimicrobial efficacy</cite>.

Title: Antimicrobial Tear Lipids in the Ocular Surface Defense
Snippet: Synergistic interactions of sphingosine with cathelicidin and LL37 against a range of Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria, and yeast have been noted (Robertson et al., 2006). Free fatty acids in skin lipids not only provide direct antibacterial activities but they enhance the antimicrobial defense of skin by inducing the expression of antimicrobial peptides in sebocytes. Incubation of sebocytes with lauric acid, palmitic acid, or oleic acid profoundly enhances expression of human b-defensin of sebocytes which shows activity against P. acnes suggesting that free fatty acids in skin lipids upregulate the expression of bdefensin in sebocytes (Nakatsuji et al., 2010). Similarly, short chain fatty acids enhance expression of antimicrobial protein, human cathelicidin LL-37 in colonocytes and play a role in mucosal immune defense (Schauber et al., 2003). 

Vernix caseosa, the creamy substance covering skin of newborns, is another example of innate host defense that is based on the cooperative interactions between antimicrobial lipids and proteins (Tollin et al., 2005). Free fatty acids in vernix exhibit antimicrobial activities and vernix lipids further enhance the activity of antimicrobial peptides indicating strong host defense resulting from interactions between antimicrobial lipids and proteins that provides protection to foetus and newborn against infections. 

The secretion of oral mucosa contains many antimicrobial salivary proteins (lysozyme, lactoferrin, lactoperoxidase), antimicrobial salivary peptides (defensins, cathelicidins, histatins), and antimicrobial salivary lipids (fatty acids derived from salivary triglycerides and long-chain bases from oral epithelial sphingolipids), and together these antimicrobial factors determine the microbial composition of the oral cavity (Wertz and de Szalay, 2020). The secretion of nasal mucosa harbours many antimicrobial proteins and lipids.

Title: Cathepsin D Is Present in Human Eccrine Sweat and Involved in the Postsecretory Processing of the Antimicrobial Peptide DCD-1L*
Snippet: Human skin serves as a first line of defense against potential pathogens by building a mechanical barrier. In addition to physical mechanisms, the epithelia of mammalian skin produce antimicrobial peptides such as cathelicidins (1,2) and ␤-defensins (3,4) or small proteins, such as the recently described 11-kDa S100 protein psoriasin (5). Cathelicidins and ␤-defensins share properties concerning their biosynthesis as proforms, which are subsequently processed into mature peptides (1,6,7). During inflammatory conditions such as wound healing (8) or psoriasis (9), the expression, processing, and secretion of the antimicrobial peptides LL-37 (10) and ␤-defensin 1 and 2 (4) are increased. As part of the innate defense of human skin the antimicrobial peptide dermcidin (DCD) is constitutively expressed in eccrine sweat glands, secreted into sweat (11), and present on the skin surface at an average concentration of 1-10 g/ml (12). In human sweat the 110-amino acid dermcidin proform is first processed to the 48-amino acid peptide DCD-1L. Subsequently DCD-1L is further C-terminal processed by a yet unidentified carboxypeptidase (13,14). 

The sole human cathelicidin hCAP-18 is extracellularly processed by proteinase 3 (15) to an active 37-amino acid peptide named LL-37, which is found in sweat at an average concentration of 0.013 M (16). After secretion, LL-37 undergoes further enzymatic processing by an unidentified serine protease yielding 3 peptides that enhance the antimicrobial activity of LL-37 itself (17). 

Beside these antimicrobial peptides and proteins, the surface of human skin provides other proteins such as human serum albumin (18), cytokeratin I (19), Zn-␣2-glycoprotein (20), prolactin-inducible protein (21), and cystatin A (22,23).

Title: An Update of the Defensive Barrier Function of Skin
Snippet: As an antimicrobial barrier against invading microorganisms, skin acts as a physical barrier and produces a number of antimicrobial peptides and proteins, including human defensins and cathelicidins. Title: The Antimicrobial Peptide AMP-IBP5 Suppresses Dermatitis-like Lesions in a Mouse Model of Atopic Dermatitis through the Low-Density Lipoprotein Receptor-Related Protein-1 Receptor
Snippet: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic inflammatory skin disease with a complex and multifactorial etiology involving genetic, immunological, and environmental factors that elicit immune dysfunction and skin barrier disruption [1,2]. Cumulative evidence has shown that, similar to immune dysfunction, disruption of the skin barrier plays a central role in the pathogenesis of AD. Impairment of tight junctions (TJs) has consistently been reported to be a key player in AD pathogenesis, as TJs interconnect with other components of the skin barrier [3][4][5]. TJs are intercellular junctions located within the stratum granulosum (SG) and comprise the claudin, occludin, and zonula occludens (ZO) protein families. TJs are thought to shape a paracellular permeability barrier regulating the passage of water, ions, and solutes [6]. De Benedetto et al. reported a significant reduction in the expression of claudin-1, an important TJ-related protein in the epidermal barrier, in subjects with AD, suggesting the deficiency of TJs in AD patients [7]. Claudin-1 deficiency was demonstrated to cause increases in transepidermal water loss (TEWL) levels in mice, accompanied by notable decreases in skin barrier function [8]. In addition, TJ barrier defects were indicated to inhibit the formation of the stratum corneum (SC) by altering polar lipid and profilaggrin processing, suggesting that TJ failure might be correlated with dysfunction of the SC barrier in AD pathogenesis [9,10]. 

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) constitute the first-line of defense in the skin against pathogens. In addition to exhibiting wide-ranging killing activity against pathogenic microorganisms, AMPs also exhibit immunomodulatory activity by inducing cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation [11]. They regulate cytokine/chemokine production, enhance angiogenesis and wound healing, and maintain skin barrier function [11][12][13][14].

Title: Topical administration of EGF suppresses immune response and protects skin barrier in DNCB-induced atopic dermatitis in NC/Nga mice
Snippet: To evaluate skin barrier function, transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and moisture retention (corneometer assay) were measured in NC/Nga mice with DNCB-induced AD-like lesions. TEWL increased and moisture retention decreased during the 21-day experimental period. TEWL of AD-like skin lesion was significantly lower in the EGF 1 and 5 ppm groups on day 21 than the control group (Fig. 2A). In addition, the corneometer score was significantly higher in EGF 1 and 5 ppm group on day 21 than in the control group (Fig. 2B). Skin barrier proteins, including tight junction (TJ) components, are involved in epidermal barrier function and prevent TEWL [17][18][19][20] . Skin barrier dysfunction could be due to defective epidermal proteins. To determine the effect of EGF on epidermal proteins in AD-like lesions, we performed immunoblotting experiments (Fig. 2C). Protein extracts were prepared from the dorsal skin of NC/Nga mice with DNCB-induced AD-like lesions. As shown in Fig. 2C, expression levels of epidermal proteins such as filaggrin, involucrin, loricrin, occludin, and ZO-1 were higher in the EGF-and PRT 0.1%-treated groups than in the control group. Furthermore, we measured the expression of filaggrin, involucrin, loricrin, and occludin in dorsal skin of mice suffering from DNCB-induced AD using immunohistochemistry (Fig. 2D,E). EGF administration increased the protein level of filaggrin, involucrin, loricrin, and occludin in DNCB-induced AD-like skin lesion. Collectively, these results support the hypothesis that EGF administration modulates skin barrier recovery by upregulating the production of epidermal proteins.

Title: Investigation of the Mechanism of Impaired Skin Barrier Function in Dogs With Malignant Tumors
Snippet: Background/Aim: No study has investigated skin barrier dysfunction with systemic diseases in veterinary medicine. We investigated the mechanism of disturbed skin barrier function in dogs with internal diseases. Materials and Methods: Healthy controls and dogs with systemic diseases were enrolled in three different disease groups: malignant tumor, hyperadrenocorticism and kidney disease. Transepidermal water loss (TEWL), serum levels of five selective pro-inflammatory cytokines and claudin-1, and complete blood count were measured. Results: TEWL was significantly increased in the malignant tumor group while serum claudin-1 concentrations were significantly lower compared to controls. Tumor necrosis factor-α was also significantly increased in the cancer group. In addition, the malignant tumor group showed significantly higher monocyte chemotactic protein-1 after chemotherapy, but lower interleukin-6 levels, compared to dogs with no chemotherapy. Conclusion: Skin barrier function was decreased in dogs with malignant tumors compared to dogs with other systemic diseases by oxidative stress and a reduction in tight junction proteins.

Title: 3-Bromo-4,5-dihydroxybenzaldehyde Isolated from Polysiphonia morrowii Suppresses TNF-α/IFN-γ-Stimulated Inflammation and Deterioration of Skin Barrier in HaCaT Keratinocytes
Snippet: The destruction of the epidermal barrier is associated with the downregulation of important protein mediators involved in skin moisturization that are crucial for the development of the barrier, such as LEKTI, filaggrin, and involucrin [3,39,40]. LEKTI is a selective inhibitor of epidermal proteinases KLK 5, 7, and 14, which perform a proinflammatory function by activating PLA-2 and IL-1β [41]. Furthermore, inflammatory responses are correlated with PAR-2 activity. IL-8 secretion is increased by PAR-2 activation via the ERK1/2 and NF-κB signaling pathways [42]. Major proteins including filaggrin and involucrin are crucial for the development of the epidermal skin barrier. Filaggrin is involved in creating a strong skin barrier and triggers the formation of molecules that helps to maintain skin hydration [43]. Involucrin improves skin barrier repair apart from the association with skin hydration [44]. In the current study, the protein levels of LEKTI, involucrin, and filaggrin were increased with BDB treatment, while the KLK5, PAR-2, and PLA-2 levels in TNF-α/IFN-γ-stimulated keratinocytes were reduced, demonstrating the anti-inflammatory potential and protective effect of BDB against the loss of skin moisturization. Moreover, the stratum granulosum contains the tight junction proteins claudins, occludin, and ZO-1, which are necessary for cell differentiation, proliferation, and the development of the permeability barrier [3]. The impairment of tight junctions is a significant contributor to the breakdown of the epidermal barrier and increases inflammatory reactions [21]. Claudins create paracellular barriers and pores that control the permeability of tight junctions [45]. The occludin can generate filaments to resemble the lacked tight junctions after translocating into the cells [46]. Additionally, ZO-1 creates cytosolic scaffolds that control tight junction construction [47].

snippet.text: Background/Aim: No study has investigated skin barrier dysfunction with systemic diseases in veterinary medicine. We investigated the mechanism of disturbed skin barrier function in dogs with internal diseases. Materials and Methods: Healthy controls and dogs with systemic diseases were enrolled in three different disease groups: malignant tumor, hyperadrenocorticism and kidney disease. Transepidermal water loss (TEWL), serum levels of five selective pro-inflammatory cytokines and claudin-1, and complete blood count were measured. Results: TEWL was significantly increased in the malignant tumor group while serum claudin-1 concentrations were significantly lower compared to controls. Tumor necrosis factor-α was also significantly increased in the cancer group. In addition, the malignant tumor group showed significantly higher monocyte chemotactic protein-1 after chemotherapy, but lower interleukin-6 levels, compared to dogs with no chemotherapy. LEKTI is a selective inhibitor of epidermal proteinases KLK 5, 7, and 14, which perform a proinflammatory function by activating PLA-2 and IL-1β [41]. Furthermore, inflammatory responses are correlated with PAR-2 activity. IL-8 secretion is increased by PAR-2 activation via the ERK1/2 and NF-κB signaling pathways [42]. Major proteins including filaggrin and involucrin are crucial for the development of the epidermal skin barrier. Filaggrin is involved in creating a strong skin barrier and triggers the formation of molecules that helps to maintain skin hydration [43]. Involucrin improves skin barrier repair apart from the association with skin hydration [44]. Claudins create paracellular barriers and pores that control the permeability of tight junctions [45]. The occludin can generate filaments to resemble the lacked tight junctions after translocating into the cells [46]. Additionally, ZO-1 creates cytosolic scaffolds that control tight junction construction [47].

documents.snippet:
Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic inflammatory skin disease with a complex and multifactorial etiology involving genetic, immunological, and environmental factors that elicit immune dysfunction and skin barrier disruption [1,2]. Cumulative evidence has shown that, similar to immune dysfunction, disruption of the skin barrier plays a central role in the pathogenesis of AD. Impairment of tight junctions (TJs) has consistently been reported to be a key player in AD pathogenesis, as TJs interconnect with other components of the skin barrier [3][4][5]. TJs are intercellular junctions located within the stratum granulosum (SG) and comprise the claudin, occludin, and zonula occludens (ZO) protein families. TJs are thought to shape a paracellular permeability barrier regulating the passage of water, ions, and solutes [6]. De Benedetto et al. reported a significant reduction in the expression of claudin-1, an important TJ-related protein in the epidermal barrier, in subjects with AD, suggesting the deficiency of TJs in AD patients [7]. Claudin-1 deficiency was demonstrated to cause increases in transepidermal water loss (TEWL) levels in mice, accompanied by notable decreases in skin barrier function [8]. In addition, TJ barrier defects were indicated to inhibit the formation of the stratum corneum (SC) by altering polar lipid and profilaggrin processing, suggesting that TJ failure might be correlated with dysfunction of the SC barrier in AD pathogenesis [9,10]. 

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) constitute the first-line of defense in the skin against pathogens. In addition to exhibiting wide-ranging killing activity against pathogenic microorganisms, AMPs also exhibit immunomodulatory activity by inducing cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation [11]. They regulate cytokine/chemokine production, enhance angiogenesis and wound healing, and maintain skin barrier function [11][12][13][14].

Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Neurogenic Inflammation of the Skin
Snippet: The skin, including the hypodermis, is the largest body organ and is in constant contact with the environment. Neurogenic inflammation is the result of the activity of nerve endings and mediators (neuropeptides secreted by nerve endings in the development of the inflammatory reaction in the skin), as well as interactions with other cells such as keratinocytes, Langerhans cells, endothelial cells and mast cells. The activation of TRPV–ion channels results in an increase in calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P, induces the release of other pro-inflammatory mediators and contributes to the maintenance of cutaneous neurogenic inflammation (CNI) in diseases such as psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, prurigo and rosacea. Immune cells present in the skin (mononuclear cells, dendritic cells and mast cells) also express TRPV1, and their activation directly affects their function. The activation of TRPV1 channels mediates communication between sensory nerve endings and skin immune cells, increasing the release of inflammatory mediators (cytokines and neuropeptides). Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the generation, activation and modulation of neuropeptide and neurotransmitter receptors in cutaneous cells can aid in the development of effective treatments for inflammatory skin disorders.

Title: Immune Actions on the Peripheral Nervous System in Pain
Snippet: Upon stimuli, injury initiates the release of inflammatory mediators (cytokines and chemokines) that cause degranulation of mast cells close to the nerve terminal, resulting in proinflammatory production. Nociceptive nerve terminals secrete neuropeptides through antidromic activation of neighboring nerve terminal branches to attract immune cells. Activated Schwann cells and neutrophils mediate breakdown of the blood-nerve barrier via the secretion of matrix metalloproteinase 9(MMP-9), promoting infiltration of immune cells including macrophages, T cells to the DRG and peripheral nerve ending. These cells, once activated, release a battery of inflammatory mediators (growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines) that act on receptors expressed on adjacent nociceptor nerve terminals, leading to nociceptor sensitization. Macrophages exhibit functions in mediating phagocytosis and tissue repair. Both macrophages and neutrophils inhibit nociceptive effects by releasing opioid peptides at injury sites.

Title: The airway neuro-immune axis as a therapeutic target in allergic airway diseases
Snippet: While higher levels of BDNF have been observed in cases of allergic rhinitis and allergic asthma, further investigations are ongoing to elucidate its impact on nerve fibers. Conversely, NGF has been previously shown to stimulate the formation of nerve fibers and facilitate the infiltration of various immune cells, such as eosinophils and lymphocytes. These immune cells, in turn, trigger Th2 cell-mediated allergic airway inflammation [25,26]. 

Neuropeptides play a pivotal role in facilitating communication between peripheral neurons and immune cells. Protease allergens, such as those from house dust mites, directly stimulate TRPV1 + sensory neurons, eliciting the release of neuropeptide SP. This neuropeptide subsequently stimulates DCs and mast cells via Mas-related G-protein coupled receptor members A1 and Mrgprb2, respectively, leading to the generation of pro-inflammatory mediators such as histamine and cytokines. This intricate process triggers additional neuropeptide release from neurons [27,28]. Consequently, the interaction between neurotransmitters or neuropeptides released by neurons and immune cells in regulating allergic airway inflammation is emerging as a prominent and intriguing area of research.

Neuroimmune interplay between nociceptors and resident immune cells are paramount in regulating host defense of peripheral tissues, such as skin, gut, and lung. Anatomical and functional studies have reported local dendritic cells (DCs) in physical proximity with nociceptors in murine skin 24 and lung mucosa. 25 TRPV1 + nociceptors elicit DC cytokine production in pathological conditions of the skin such as psoriasis 26 fungal infection. 27 Local macrophages are spatially associated with peripheral nerve fibers, 28 phagocytose myelin debris, [29][30][31] and have also been shown to interact with TRPV1 + nociceptors in skin and pancreas to modulate inflammatory macrophage recruitment [32][33][34] and phagocytosis of microbial pathogens. 35 he cornea contains resident DCs in the epithelium and macrophages in the stroma that contribute to host defense of the ocular surface. Emerging anatomical evidence has shown the physical proximity of corneal immune cells with intraepithelial nerve fibers 36 and with large limbal nerve trunks in the stroma. 37 Pharmacological depletion of DCs lowers the intraepithelial nerve fiber density. 36 This interdependence of corneal nerves and DCs is facilitated by DC-mediated production of ciliary neurotrophic factor, which enhances nerve regeneration after epithelial injury. 38 hile the studies detailed above clearly demonstrate the existence of TRPV1 + nerves in the mouse cornea, their anatomical distribution and their relationships with the local immune cells during homeostasis and injury remains uncharacterized. In this study we demonstrated a close physical proximity exists between TRPV1 + nerves and resident immune cells, and report punctate intracellular TRPV1 expression within stromal macrophages. This anatomical nociceptor-immune axis may be involved in corneal pain responses following injury at the ocular surface.

Title: The role of psychological stress in the pathogenesis of psoriasis
Snippet: The skin is innervated by at least three types of nerve fibers, i.e., A, B, and C fibers, exerting sensation and regulation of cutaneous functions through secretion of neuropeptides and neurotrophins (139). In addition to upregulation of expression levels of nerve growth factor and its receptors in the skin (140), psychological stress increases circulating levels of nerve growth factor by over 80% (141). Nerve growth factor stimulates proliferation of neuron/non-neuron cells, including keratinocytes and fibroblasts, while inhibiting keratinocyte apoptosis, a feature of psoriasis (142,143). Moreover, nerve growth factor induces inflammation via stimulation of degranulation and cytokine release from mast cells in the skin (143). Application of neutralizing nerve growth factor antibody decreases number of degranulated mast cells in the dermis and subcutaneous tissues of sonic stressed mice (139). Psoriatic skin expresses high levels of nerve growth factor and its receptors along with increased nerve innervation (144). In addition, nerve growth factor stimulates angiogenesis, upregulates expression levels of adhesion molecules, and activates T cells (143). The role of nerve growth factor in the pathogenesis of psoriasis is further supported by the evidence that inhibition of nerve growth factor receptor with either its blocker or its neutralizing antibody improves psoriasis (145). Hence, stress-induced increases in nerve growth factor can contribute, in part, to the pathogenesis of psoriasis. 

Psychological stress also increases substance P in the brain (146), which then is transported to peripheral nerve terminals (147). Substance P and its receptors also express in various types of immune cells such as mast cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, T cells and monocytes. Studies showed that substance P induces infiltration of neutrophils in the skin and increases chemokine and chemokine receptor expression in primary mouse neutrophils.

documents.snippet: Upon stimuli, injury initiates the release of inflammatory mediators (cytokines and chemokines) that cause degranulation of mast cells close to the nerve terminal, resulting in proinflammatory production. Nociceptive nerve terminals secrete neuropeptides through antidromic activation of neighboring nerve terminal branches to attract immune cells. Activated Schwann cells and neutrophils mediate breakdown of the blood-nerve barrier via the secretion of matrix metalloproteinase 9(MMP-9), promoting infiltration of immune cells including macrophages, T cells to the DRG and peripheral nerve ending. These cells, once activated, release a battery of inflammatory mediators (growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines) that act on receptors expressed on adjacent nociceptor nerve terminals, leading to nociceptor sensitization. Macrophages exhibit functions in mediating phagocytosis and tissue repair. Both macrophages and neutrophils inhibit nociceptive effects by releasing opioid peptides at injury sites.

documents.title: The airway neuro-immune axis as a therapeutic target in allergic airway diseases
documents.snippet:
While higher levels of BDNF have been observed in cases of allergic rhinitis and allergic asthma, further investigations are ongoing to elucidate its impact on nerve fibers. Conversely, NGF has been previously shown to stimulate the formation of nerve fibers and facilitate the infiltration of various immune cells, such as eosinophils and lymphocytes. These immune cells, in turn, trigger Th2 cell-mediated allergic airway inflammation [25,26]. 

Neuropeptides play a pivotal role in facilitating communication between peripheral neurons and immune cells. Protease allergens, such as those from house dust mites, directly stimulate TRPV1 + sensory neurons, eliciting the release of neuropeptide SP. This neuropeptide subsequently stimulates DCs and mast cells via Mas-related G-protein coupled receptor members A1 and Mrgprb2, respectively, leading to the generation of pro-inflammatory mediators such as histamine and cytokines. This intricate process triggers additional neuropeptide release from neurons [27,28]. Consequently, the interaction between neurotransmitters or neuropeptides released by neurons and immune cells in regulating allergic airway inflammation is emerging as a prominent and intriguing area of research.

documents.title: Distribution of Corneal TRPV1 and Its Association With Immune Cells During Homeostasis and Injury
documents.snippet:
However, the relative rate of recovery of TRPV1 + nerve fibers was not examined. 

Neuroimmune interplay between nociceptors and resident immune cells are paramount in regulating host defense of peripheral tissues, such as skin, gut, and lung. Anatomical and functional studies have reported local dendritic cells (DCs) in physical proximity with nociceptors in murine skin 24 and lung mucosa. 25 TRPV1 + nociceptors elicit DC cytokine production in pathological conditions of the skin such as psoriasis 26 fungal infection. 27 Local macrophages are spatially associated with peripheral nerve fibers, 28 phagocytose myelin debris, [29][30][31] and have also been shown to interact with TRPV1 + nociceptors in skin and pancreas to modulate inflammatory macrophage recruitment [32][33][34] and phagocytosis of microbial pathogens. 35 he cornea contains resident DCs in the epithelium and macrophages in the stroma that contribute to host defense of the ocular surface. Emerging anatomical evidence has shown the physical proximity of corneal immune cells with intraepithelial nerve fibers 36 and with large limbal nerve trunks in the stroma. 37 Pharmacological depletion of DCs lowers the intraepithelial nerve fiber density. 36 This interdependence of corneal nerves and DCs is facilitated by DC-mediated production of ciliary neurotrophic factor, which enhances nerve regeneration after epithelial injury. 38 hile the studies detailed above clearly demonstrate the existence of TRPV1 + nerves in the mouse cornea, their anatomical distribution and their relationships with the local immune cells during homeostasis and injury remains uncharacterized. In this study we demonstrated a close physical proximity exists between TRPV1 + nerves and resident immune cells, and report punctate intracellular TRPV1 expression within stromal macrophages. This anatomical nociceptor-immune axis may be involved in corneal pain responses following injury at the ocular surface.

documents.title: The role of psychological stress in the pathogenesis of psoriasis
documents.snippet:
The skin is innervated by at least three types of nerve fibers, i.e., A, B, and C fibers, exerting sensation and regulation of cutaneous functions through secretion of neuropeptides and neurotrophins (139). In addition to upregulation of expression levels of nerve growth factor and its receptors in the skin (140), psychological stress increases circulating levels of nerve growth factor by over 80% (141). Nerve growth factor stimulates proliferation of neuron/non-neuron cells, including keratinocytes and fibroblasts, while inhibiting keratinocyte apoptosis, a feature of psoriasis (142,143). Moreover, nerve growth factor induces inflammation via stimulation of degranulation and cytokine release from mast cells in the skin (143). Application of neutralizing nerve growth factor antibody decreases number of degranulated mast cells in the dermis and subcutaneous tissues of sonic stressed mice (139). Psoriatic skin expresses high levels of nerve growth factor and its receptors along with increased nerve innervation (144). In addition, nerve growth factor stimulates angiogenesis, upregulates expression levels of adhesion molecules, and activates T cells (143). The role of nerve growth factor in the pathogenesis of psoriasis is further supported by the evidence that inhibition of nerve growth factor receptor with either its blocker or its neutralizing antibody improves psoriasis (145). Hence, stress-induced increases in nerve growth factor can contribute, in part, to the pathogenesis of psoriasis. 

Psychological stress also increases substance P in the brain (146), which then is transported to peripheral nerve terminals (147). Substance P and its receptors also express in various types of immune cells such as mast cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, T cells and monocytes. Studies showed that substance P induces infiltration of neutrophils in the skin and increases chemokine and chemokine receptor expression in primary mouse neutrophils.
